title: Risk-based regulatory approach and scope
text: The EU AI Act regulates AI using a risk-based approach. Obligations depend on the system’s risk category and the actor’s role (provider, deployer, importer, distributor). Start by mapping the system, role(s), and where it is placed on the market or put into service, then decide which obligations apply.

title: Clear allocation of roles and responsibilities
text: Clearly determine who is the provider vs deployer vs importer/distributor for the AI system and document the rationale. Assign internal accountable owners for each role-related duty (documentation, monitoring, incident handling). A weak role map produces governance ambiguity and breaks auditability.

title: Identify prohibited AI practices early
text: Screen the use case against prohibited AI practices before investing further. If the use falls within prohibited practices, the only viable outcome is redesign, scope reduction, or non-deployment. Keep a short decision memo showing what was checked and why it is not prohibited (or how it was redesigned).

title: High-risk classification decision and documentation
text: Decide whether the system qualifies as high-risk based on intended purpose and deployment context. Record the classification rationale, boundaries (what is and is not in scope), and the operational scenario. Treat this as a primary evidence artifact, because downstream obligations depend on it.

title: Lifecycle risk management system
text: Maintain a continuous risk management process across design, development, deployment, and post-market monitoring. Document hazards, likelihood/impact, mitigations, residual risk decisions, and review cadence. Risk management is not a one-time checklist; it is a maintained operational loop.

title: Data governance and quality controls
text: Implement data governance to ensure data relevance, representativeness, quality, and provenance. Identify bias risks from sampling, labeling, and deployment population mismatch, then document mitigations. Track data lineage and changes so performance shifts can be explained and audited.

title: Technical documentation as audit evidence
text: Maintain technical documentation describing purpose, design, model/data choices, evaluation, limitations, and operational controls. Tie each major risk to specific evidence (tests, logs, approvals) and control owners. The goal is not paperwork; it is reproducible system understanding.

title: Record-keeping and logging for traceability
text: Enable logs and records sufficient for traceability, incident investigation, and accountability. Define what events are logged (inputs/outputs/decisions/overrides), who can access logs, and retention rules. Logging should support ‘why did this happen’ without creating unnecessary privacy exposure.

title: User transparency and instructions for use
text: Provide instructions and transparency information so deployers/operators can use the system correctly. Include limitations, intended purpose, known failure modes, and recommended human oversight. Transparency is operational: it reduces misuse and clarifies appropriate reliance.

title: Human oversight design and operationalization
text: Specify when humans must review, override, or intervene, and what authority they have. Define operator training, escalation paths, and how overrides are logged. Oversight must be practical (who, when, how), not just a policy statement.

title: Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity expectations
text: Define performance expectations aligned with risk, and implement safeguards against attacks, misuse, and degradation. Include threat modeling for AI-specific risks (prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction) where relevant. Track robustness over time so drift is observable and explainable.

title: Conformity assessment readiness (evidence packaging)
text: Prepare evidence artifacts so a conformity assessment can be supported: documentation, testing, QMS processes, monitoring plan, and incident handling. Maintain an ‘evidence index’ that maps obligations to artifacts and owners. The key deliverable is a coherent audit trail, not isolated files.

title: Post-market monitoring plan
text: Define how real-world performance and harms are monitored after deployment. Include drift detection, abuse signals, user feedback channels, and periodic review. Monitoring must connect to actions: thresholds, rollback/fallback, and governance escalation when issues appear.

title: Serious incident reporting and corrective actions
text: Define what counts as a serious incident, how it is detected, who triages it, and how corrective actions are tracked. Establish communication steps and documentation templates so response is fast and consistent. Incident readiness is a core part of organizational explainability: ‘what happened and what we did’.

title: GPAI responsibilities awareness (integration governance)
text: When integrating general-purpose models, document capabilities, limitations, and intended use boundaries. Establish integration controls: prompt/version control, evaluation, monitoring, and fallback. Treat model integration as a managed dependency with owners and change governance.

title: Transparency measures for generative AI outputs
text: Implement transparency measures for AI-generated content where applicable, including user awareness and provenance support. Clarify when users are interacting with AI and what limitations apply. For higher-risk contexts, add friction: disclaimers, human review, and escalation paths.

title: Governance: policies, roles, and controls
text: Establish internal governance policies and role definitions covering approvals, change control, monitoring, and incident response. Require decision logs for exceptions and risk acceptance. Governance exists to make decisions explainable, repeatable, and reviewable.

title: Quality management system alignment
text: Use a structured quality management approach to ensure repeatable development and accountable change management. Define what counts as a ‘material change’ and what re-evaluation it triggers. QMS turns AI development from ad-hoc to explainable operational practice.

title: Supply chain and third-party assurance
text: Assess third-party components (models, data, tools) and require documentation and security assurances. Define procurement gates for AI dependencies and track versions used in production. Supply chain governance is essential to explain incidents and accountability across vendors.

title: Change management and versioning
text: Track changes to model, data, prompts, policies, and runtime configuration. For material changes, re-assess risks, re-run evaluations, and update documentation. Versioning is the backbone of ‘why did the output change’ explanations.

title: Intended purpose and foreseeable misuse
text: Define intended purpose and identify foreseeable misuse scenarios. Build controls that specifically address misuse (rate limits, safety filters, human escalation, monitoring). ‘Foreseeable misuse’ should be documented as scenarios with detection signals and mitigations.

title: Testing and evaluation evidence
text: Run pre-deployment evaluations aligned with the risk profile and usage context. Document test design, datasets, metrics, stress tests, and results. Evaluation evidence should connect to go/no-go decisions and residual risk acceptance logs.

title: Operator training and competency
text: Ensure operators understand system limitations, appropriate reliance, and incident handling procedures. Provide training materials and confirm competency for high-impact contexts. Training artifacts can be part of explainability: ‘we enabled humans to oversee effectively’.

title: Logging design with privacy/security constraints
text: Design logs to support traceability while minimizing personal data exposure. Apply access controls, retention limits, and redaction strategies for sensitive content. Logging must be both useful for investigation and safe under privacy/security constraints.

title: Operational incident response for AI failures
text: Define triage procedures, rollback/fallback mechanisms, communication plans, and remediation tracking for AI incidents and vulnerabilities. Ensure incident response integrates with monitoring signals and governance escalation. The output should be a reproducible incident narrative with evidence links.
